title: Imports and Dependencies
content: The formalization imports Mathlib's finset cardinality, natural number basics, and general tactic support. These provide the combinatorial infrastructure for reasoning about finite point sets and their subsets.
mathContext: We work with $\text{Finset}(\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R})$ and use cardinality $|S|$ for counting.

title: Planar Point Set
content: A PlanarPointSet is a nonempty finite subset of the Euclidean plane. The nonemptiness condition (size_pos) ensures the set contains at least one point, which is needed for well-definedness of counting arguments.
mathContext: $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with $|P| > 0$, represented as a finset of pairs $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$.

title: Collinearity via Signed Area
content: Three points are collinear if and only if the signed area of the triangle they form vanishes. This is equivalent to the cross product of the displacement vectors being zero, which is the standard determinant test for collinearity in the plane.

title: No Five Collinear Condition
content: The point set has no five collinear points: for any five distinct points in P, they cannot all lie on a single line. This is the precise threshold condition for Problem #101. If five collinear points were allowed, one could place n points on two lines, immediately getting $\Omega(n^2)$ four-point lines (by choosing 3 from one line and 1 from the other), making the o(n^2) question trivial. The formalization quantifies over all 5-element subsets and checks that not all pairwise collinearity relations hold simultaneously.
mathContext: No five distinct $a, b, c, d, e \in P$ satisfy $\text{collinear}(a,b,c) \wedge \text{collinear}(a,b,d) \wedge \text{collinear}(a,b,e)$ simultaneously.

title: Four-Point Line Count
content: Counts the number of 4-element subsets of P that are collinear (all four points on a common line). The definition filters the powerset of P for subsets of size 4 where there exist two distinct points a, b in the subset such that all four points are collinear with a and b. For no-five-collinear sets, each four-point line contributes exactly one such subset.
mathContext: $f_4(P) = |\{S \subseteq P : |S| = 4, \exists\, a \neq b \in S,\, \forall p \in S,\, \text{collinear}(a, b, p)\}|$

title: Erdos Problem #101: The o(n^2) Conjecture
content: The central conjecture: for any $\varepsilon > 0$, sufficiently large no-five-collinear point sets have fewer than $\varepsilon n^2$ four-point lines. This is an asymptotic statement using little-o notation, formalized via the epsilon-N_0 definition. Erdos offered $100 for its resolution. The conjecture remains open, with the best known lower bound being nearly quadratic (Solymosi-Stojakovic), leaving open whether the count can truly be subquadratic.
mathContext: $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\, \exists N_0,\, \forall P$ with $|P| \geq N_0$ and no five collinear: $f_4(P) < \varepsilon \cdot |P|^2$.

title: Grunbaum's Lower Bound Construction
content: Grunbaum constructed explicit no-five-collinear point sets achieving $\gg n^{3/2}$ four-point lines. His construction uses lattice-based configurations and algebraic curves to ensure many collinear quadruples while avoiding five-point collinearities. This was the basis for Erdos's original conjecture that the true order is $\Theta(n^{3/2})$, which was later disproved by Solymosi and Stojakovic.
mathContext: $\exists c > 0,\, \forall N,\, \exists P$ with no five collinear, $|P| \geq N$, and $f_4(P) \geq c \cdot |P|^{3/2}$.

title: Solymosi-Stojakovic: Nearly Quadratic Lower Bound
content: Solymosi and Stojakovic dramatically improved Grunbaum's lower bound by constructing point sets with $n^{2 - O(1/\sqrt{\log n})}$ four-point lines while maintaining the no-five-collinear condition. This disproved Erdos's original $\Theta(n^{3/2})$ conjecture and pushed the known lower bound to within a subpolynomial factor of the trivial $O(n^2)$ upper bound. Their construction uses sophisticated combinatorial and probabilistic techniques.
mathContext: $\forall C > 0,\, \exists N_0,\, \forall n \geq N_0,\, \exists P$ with $|P| = n$, no five collinear, and $f_4(P) \geq n^{2 - C/\sqrt{\log n}}$.

title: Trivial Quadratic Upper Bound
content: Any n points determine at most $\binom{n}{2} = n(n-1)/2$ lines, so the number of four-point lines is at most $O(n^2)$. This is the trivial upper bound. The key question is whether an o(n^2) bound holds, i.e., whether the count is asymptotically smaller than any constant fraction of $n^2$.

title: Collinear Triples without Four-Point Lines
content: Burr, Grunbaum, and Sloane, and independently Furedi and Palasti, constructed point sets with approximately $n^2/6$ collinear triples but no line containing four or more points. This shows that having many collinear triples does not force four-point lines, highlighting the delicate combinatorial distinction between 3-collinear and 4-collinear configurations.
mathContext: $\exists c > 0,\, \forall N,\, \exists P$ with $|P| \geq N$, no five collinear, and $f_4(P) = 0$ (while having $\sim |P|^2/6$ collinear triples).

title: Szemeredi-Trotter Incidence Bound
content: The Szemeredi-Trotter theorem (1983) bounds the number of point-line incidences: given n points and m lines in the plane, the number of incidences is $O(n^{2/3}m^{2/3} + n + m)$. This is tight and is one of the most powerful tools in combinatorial geometry. For four-point lines, applying Szemeredi-Trotter to n points and m four-rich lines gives a relationship constraining the count. The theorem was originally proved using a cell decomposition of the plane.
mathContext: $I(P, L) \leq C(|P|^{2/3}|L|^{2/3} + |P| + |L|)$ for some absolute constant $C > 0$.
